identity.title: Molecular Line Observations in Two Dusty Star-forming Galaxies at z = 6.9

paper_type_evidence.quote: In this paper, we present a detailed analysis of the molecular interstellar medium at z = 6.9, through high resolution observations of the $\rm CO(6-5)$, $\rm CO(7-6)$, $\rm CO(10-9)$, \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$, and p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ lines and dust continuum emission with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).
We obtained observations of different emission lines and the continuum using ALMA Band 3 and 4 over three tunings (Project ID: 2017.1.01168.S, PI: Vieira).

question.value: What are the physical properties of the molecular interstellar medium, gas mass, CO-to-H2 conversion factor, gas depletion timescales, and heating mechanisms in the two dusty star-forming galaxies of SPT0311-58 at z = 6.9?

evidence.quote: In this paper, we present a detailed analysis of the molecular interstellar medium at z = 6.9, through high resolution observations of the $\rm CO(6-5)$, $\rm CO(7-6)$, $\rm CO(10-9)$, \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$, and p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ lines and dust continuum emission with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).
We use realistic non-Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium (non-LTE) models and estimate the physical properties of the ISM in both the galaxies.
We obtained observations of different emission lines and the continuum using ALMA Band 3 and 4 over three tunings (Project ID: 2017.1.01168.S, PI: Vieira).
The source has been observed in previous ALMA cycles (2015.1.00504.S, PI: Strandet and 2016.1.01293.S, PI: Marrone) in B3, B6, B7, and B8 corresponding to 95, 240, 340, and 420 GHz, respectively.

analysis_steps.goal: Image continuum and spectral lines and extract 1D spectra

method.value: Image continuum by combining LSB and USB excluding line channels; subtract continuum in uv-plane using uvcontsub (order 1); image spectral cubes at 100 km/s resolution and single-channel moment 0 maps; extract 1D spectra using apertures of 2.5'' (W) and 1.2'' (E).

evidence.quote: The continuum images are produced by combining the lower and upper side bands (LSB, USB) and excluding the channels containing the line emission.

To generate the spectral cubes, we use the same weighting as with the continuum maps and a velocity averaging of 100 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$, after subtracting the continuum using `CASA` task `uvcontsub` with a polynomial fit of order 1.
The spectra in W and E are extracted from the 100 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ spectral cubes using an aperture of 2.5$\ensuremath{''}$ and 1.2$\ensuremath{''}$, respectively.
Briggs weighting and a robust parameter of 0.5 are used, which provide a good compromise between resolution and noise.

key_parameters.value: Spectral cube velocity averaging = 100 km s^-1; Moment 0 single channel width = 1000 km s^-1 (W) and 500 km s^-1 (E)

evidence.quote: To generate the velocity integrated intensity maps (moment 0), we produce single channel cubes with a width of 1000 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ in W and 500 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ in E, which is $\sim$2 $\times$ full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the lines.
The spectra in W and E are extracted from the 100 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ spectral cubes using an aperture of 2.5$\ensuremath{''}$ and 1.2$\ensuremath{''}$, respectively.

evidence.quote: We consider a velocity separation of $\sim$750 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ between W and E based on the high resolution \[CII\] observations (cite: marrone18).

analysis_steps.goal: Decompose blended and non-Gaussian spectral lines and calculate line luminosities

method.value: Re-image ALMA 240 GHz [CII] data with the same weighting and velocity averaging to use as a high-SNR template; scale the [CII] template to observed line spectra (jointly for blended lines) via least squares; integrate flux from line center - 3*sigma_v to + 3*sigma_v; repeat 3000 times with random Gaussian noise to get median and standard deviation; convert I_obs to L_line and L'_line using Solomon et al. (1997) equations.

evidence.quote: Since the spectral lines are non-Gaussian and blended in the case of $\rm CO(7-6)$ and \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$, and $\rm CO(10-9)$ and p-$\rm H_{2} O (3_{1,2}-2_{2,1})$, we use \[CII\] from the ALMA 240 GHz observations (cite: marrone18) as a template to derive the spectral properties.
We estimate the line properties by repeating the scaling 3000 times with random Gaussian noise added to the flux density and taking the median value of all the fits.

key_parameters.value: [CII] template FWHM = 779 +/- 25 km s^-1 (W) and 371 +/- 12 km s^-1 (E)

evidence.quote: The \[CII\] spectrum obtained has a FWHM of 779 $\pm$ 25 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ in W and 371 $\pm$ 12 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ in E.

key_parameters.value: Integration range: line center - 3*sigma_v to line center + 3*sigma_v; 3000 Monte Carlo iterations

evidence.quote: We estimate the line properties by repeating the scaling 3000 times with random Gaussian noise added to the flux density and taking the median value of all the fits.

assumptions.value: Molecular lines share the same kinematic profile as the [CII] template; unresolved ATCA CO(3-2) flux distributed between W and E by scaling to CO(6-5); flat LambdaCDM cosmology (h = 0.677, Omega_m = 0.307, Omega_Lambda = 0.693)

evidence.quote: We use flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology where $h$ = 0.677, $\Omega_{m}$ = 0.307, and $\Omega_{\Lambda}$ = 0.693 (cite: planck16cosmo).
Since $\rm CO(3-2)$ is spatially unresolved ($\sim$5 $-$ 6$''$) into W and E, we distribute the flux density of $\rm CO(3-2)$ by scaling to $\rm CO(6-5)$ in the two galaxies.

fitting.value: Least squares fit of scaled [CII] template with 3000 Monte Carlo noise realizations

evidence.quote: This \[CII\] spectrum is scaled to the observed spectrum of the lines using a least squares fit.
We estimate the line properties by repeating the scaling 3000 times with random Gaussian noise added to the flux density and taking the median value of all the fits.

analysis_steps.goal: Perform gravitational lens modeling in the visibility plane

method.value: Fit parametric lens models to visibility data of 140 GHz and 101 GHz continuum and single-channel (1000 km/s) CO(6-5), CO(7-6), and CO(10-9) lines in W using visilens with SIE lens profile and Sersic source profile(s).

evidence.quote: In this analysis, we perform lens modeling on the 140 and 101 GHz ($\sim$272 and 375 $\mu$m rest-frame, respectively) continuum, and $\rm CO(6-5)$, $\rm CO(7-6)$, and $\rm CO(10-9)$ molecular line transitions in W.
Since the signal-to-noise is not sufficiently high for pixellated modeling, we use a parametric lens modeling code, `visilens` (cite: spilker16).
For the lines, we fit single channel models with the width of 1000 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$, which is equivalent to the $\sim$2 $\times$ FWHM to estimate the overall magnification.

key_parameters.value: 1000 MCMC chains; lens parameters constrained within best-fit values of 140 GHz single-lens model

evidence.quote: As the best-fit parameters, we take the median value of the 1000 MCMC chains with 1$\sigma$ uncertainty.
For all the lensing reconstruction in this paper, we vary the lens parameters only within the best-fit values obtained from the high resolution 140 GHz measurement set using a single lens.

assumptions.value: SIE lens mass profile, Sersic source profile; fixed magnification mu = 1.3 for E and mu = 2.2 for p-H2O in W from Marrone et al. (2018)

evidence.quote: In this code, the background source is parameterized by one or more S$\rm \acute{e}$rsic (cite: sersic68) profiles with seven free parameters: source position relative to the lens ($\rm x_{S}, y_{S}$), flux density (S), half light radius major axis ($\rm a_{S}$), S$\rm \acute{e}$rsic index ($\rm n_{S}$), axis ratio ($\rm b_{S}/a_{S}$), and position angle ($\rm \phi_{S}$).

The lensing source is represented by one or more Singular Isothermal Ellipsoids (SIEs), which has five free parameters: the center of the lens relative to phase center ($\rm x_{L}$, $\rm y_{L}$), the lens mass ($\rm M_{L}$) which determines the strength of lensing, the ellipticity of the lens ($\rm e_{L}$), and the position angle of the lens major axis ($\rm \phi_{L}$) in degrees east of north.

Since we do not have a good signal-to-noise for lensing reconstruction in E, we adopt a magnification of 1.3 for all the molecular lines. For the same reason, we adopt $\mu = 2.2$ from (cite: marrone18) in p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ in W.

fitting.value: MCMC sampling (emcee) in the visibility plane; Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) used to select number of sources

evidence.quote: This model uses a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm (`emcee` package; (cite: foremanmackey13)) to sample the parameter space.
The performance of different models is measured by Deviance Information Criterion (DIC; (cite: spiegelhalter02)) to determine the number of sources to include in the model.

validation.value: 140 GHz lens parameters compared and found to agree with Marrone et al. (2018) pixellated lens model

evidence.quote: The lens parameters obtained from the 140 GHz data agree with (cite: marrone18) model.

analysis_steps.goal: Fit modified blackbody dust SED to derive dust temperature, dust mass, L_FIR, and L_IR

method.value: Fit a uniform-temperature modified blackbody function (including CMB effect) to magnification-corrected rest-frame >50 um photometry using MCMC to sample M_dust and T_dust, then integrate rest-frame 8-1000 um for L_IR and 42.5-122.5 um for L_FIR.

evidence.quote: We estimate the $\rm L_{IR}$ as flux integrated from 8$-$1000 $\rm \mu m$ and total far-infrared luminosity ($\rm L_{FIR}$) from 42.5$-$122.5 $\rm \mu m$ in the rest frame (cite: helou85).

In this section, we assume a uniform dust temperature ($\rm T_{dust}$) in each source and fit a modified blackbody function to the photometry greater than 50 $\mu m$ rest frame and the equations are adopted from (cite: weiss07):
We use MCMC algorithm to sample the dust mass and the dust temperature by giving an upper limit on the effective radius as 5000 pc in W and 1300 pc in E.

key_parameters.value: 15% calibration/lensing error added in quadrature; upper limit on effective radius = 5000 pc (W) and 1300 pc (E)

evidence.quote: A 15% absolute calibration error is added in quadrature to the statistical error to account for the uncertainty from the absolute flux calibration and lens modeling.
We use MCMC algorithm to sample the dust mass and the dust temperature by giving an upper limit on the effective radius as 5000 pc in W and 1300 pc in E.

assumptions.value: Uniform dust temperature; kappa_nu = 0.038 * (nu / 372.7 GHz)^beta_Td [m^2 kg^-1] from Draine (2003); beta_Td fixed to 2.0

evidence.quote: The frequency dependent dust absorption coefficient is adopted from (cite: draine03) $$\begin{equation}\rm \kappa_{\nu} = 0.038(\nu/372.7 \ GHz)^{\beta_{T_{d}}} \ [m^{2} \ kg^{-1}] \end{equation}$$
We fix $\beta_{T_{d}}$ to 2.0 (cite: greve12).

fitting.value: MCMC sampling of M_dust and T_dust

evidence.quote: We use MCMC algorithm to sample the dust mass and the dust temperature by giving an upper limit on the effective radius as 5000 pc in W and 1300 pc in E.

validation.value: Derived L_IR and L_FIR agree with CIGALE SED fits from Marrone et al. (2018) within uncertainties

evidence.quote: These values agree with the luminosities inferred from `CIGALE` SED fits from (cite: marrone18) to within the uncertainties.

analysis_steps.goal: Analyze L_H2O - L_FIR correlation and derive H2O-based SFR and [CI]-based gas mass

method.value: Perform MCMC linear regression of log10(L_H2O/L_FIR) vs log10(L_FIR) across SPT0311-58 and literature sample; calibrate Kennicutt & Evans (2012) SFR relation with L_H2O; calculate molecular gas mass from [CI](2-1) luminosity using Weiss et al. (2003, 2005) equation with CMB correction.

evidence.quote: To get the correlation between $\rm L_{H_{2}O}$ and $\rm L_{FIR}$, we perform two MCMC linear regressions to all the sources in log-log space as shown in Figure 3.
We calibrate this SFR with $\rm L_{H_{2}O}$ using $\rm L_{IR}$/$\rm L_{FIR}$ values from the SED fit and Equation \[eqn:lh2o_lfir\].
where $\rm T_{1}$ = 23.6 K and $\rm T_{2}$ = 62.5 K are the excitation energy transitions of the two transitions of \[CI\].

assumptions.value: No differential magnification between H2O and continuum; SFR [M_sun/yr] = 1.47e-10 L_IR [L_sun]; T_ex = 30 K for [CI]; [CI]/[H2] = (8.4 +/- 3.5)e-5; Helium correction factor = 1.36

evidence.quote: We assume that there is no differential magnification between $\rm H_{2}O$ and continuum emission in the gravitationally lensed sources.
However, since we only have observations of \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$, we adopt a typical value of $\rm T_{ex}$ = 30 K (cite: walter11).

The gas mass from \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$ is converted into the total $\rm H_{2}$ gas mass by assuming $\rm [CI]/[H_{2}]$ abundance of (8.4 $\pm$ 3.5) $\times 10^{-5}$ (cite: walter11). To include the contribution from Helium, we multiply the $\rm H_{2}$ gas mass by 1.36.

fitting.value: MCMC linear regression in log-log space (with slope fixed to zero and slope free)

evidence.quote: To get the correlation between $\rm L_{H_{2}O}$ and $\rm L_{FIR}$, we perform two MCMC linear regressions to all the sources in log-log space as shown in Figure 3.

validation.value: H2O-based SFR and [CI]-based gas mass compared against L_IR-based SFR and LVG radiative transfer model outputs

evidence.quote: Both the calculations give consistent values within errors in W.
The gas mass estimated from \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$ agrees with the LVG models to within the uncertainties.

analysis_steps.goal: Perform non-LTE LVG radiative transfer modeling of dust, CO, and [CI] simultaneously

method.value: Simultaneously fit dust continuum, CO SLED, and [CI](2-1) flux densities using non-LTE LVG radiative transfer models (1-component, 2-component, and Turbulence models, where Turbulence samples 50 densities from a log-normal PDF) optimized via the Monte Carlo Bees Algorithm.

evidence.quote: To model the dust emission, observed CO, and \[CI\] flux densities in SPT0311-58 W and E, we use two non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) large velocity gradient (LVG) radiative transfer modeling methods: *N-component* and *Turbulence*.
For each value of $\rm < n_{H_{2}}>$, we sample 50 gas densities within $\rm 10 - 10^{10} \ cm^{-3}$. The final dust and gas SED, which describes the observations, is the sum of all the 50 SEDs.
The models are optimized to fit the observed flux densities of dust and gas using the Monte Carlo Bees Algorithm (cite: pham09).

key_parameters.value: 10 input parameters (1-component), 20 input parameters (2-component), 12 input parameters (Turbulence); 30 independent runs evaluating ~10^7 models total

evidence.quote: This model will henceforth be referred to as *1-component* and *2-component*, which has 10 and 20 input parameters, respectively (see Table \[ncomp_parameters\] in the Appendix). The *Turbulence* model realistically models the ISM with 12 input parameters (see Table \[turb_parameters\]).
We run the code 30 times to avoid artificially narrow PDFs for the solutions and hence have 30 final solutions.

We evaluate $\sim$10$^{7}$ models and the best-fit *Turbulence* model parameter values shown in Table \[turb_parameters\] are obtained by taking the mean and standard deviation from all the model runs.

key_parameters.value: Parameter priors/ranges in Table 3: log(n_H2) in [1, 7], T_K in [21, 600] K, T_K/T_dust in [0.5, 6.0], beta_TK in [-0.5, -0.05], beta_Tdust in [1.5, 2.0], R_eff in [0.1, 5000] pc, kappa_vir in [1, 3], dv_turb in [5, 200] km/s, GDMR in [90, 1100] (or [120, 150] for Z_sun), [CO/H2] in [1e-7, 2e-4] (or [1e-4, 2e-4] for Z_sun), [CI/H2] in [1e-7, 1e-4], beta_[CI] in [-5, 0]

assumptions.value: Dust opacity kappa_nu / m^2 kg^-1 = 0.04 * (nu / 250 GHz)^beta_Td; log-normal density PDF in supersonically isothermal turbulent gas; T_K and [CI] abundance coupled to density as power laws in Turbulence model; Helium factor 1.36

evidence.quote: In the radiative transfer models, we adopt $\rm \kappa_{\nu}/m^{2}\ kg^{-1}\ = 0.04 \times (\nu/250\ GHz)^{\beta_{T_{d}}}$.

$\rm dp(n^{\prime}, dv_{turb})$ is the log-normal probability distribution function (PDF) in supersonically isothermal turbulent gas as given in (cite: krumholz05), which depends on the normalized gas density ($\rm n^{\prime}$) and the turbulence line width ($\rm dv_{turb}$).

The turbulence line width along the line of sight, in addition to the other free parameters, determine the gas mass including the contribution from Helium (cite: weiss07), which is given by: $$\begin{equation}\label{gasmasseqn} \rm M_{gas} = 1.36 \ \Omega \ \frac{n_{H_{2}}}{dv/dr} \ dv_{turb}\end{equation}$$

fitting.value: Monte Carlo Bees Algorithm optimizing chi^2 across 30 runs (~10^7 models); best-fit parameters and errors are chi^2-weighted mean and standard deviation

evidence.quote: The models are optimized to fit the observed flux densities of dust and gas using the Monte Carlo Bees Algorithm (cite: pham09).

The best-fit value for each parameter is taken as the mean of outputs from all the 10$^{7}$ models weighted by $\chi^{2}$, and the error on the parameters is the $\chi^{2}$ weighted standard deviation.

validation.value: Compared 1-component, 2-component, and Turbulence models, and tested sub-solar vs solar metallicity constraints and sensitivity to CO(13-12) upper limits

evidence.quote: We also include these upper limits in the *1-component* and *Turbulence* models, although the results do not change significantly when the limits are not included.
The total gas mass from the *2-component* models is consistent with the *Turbulence* models within uncertainties.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive alpha_CO, gas depletion timescales, and neutral gas energy budget

method.value: Calculate alpha_CO = M_gas / L'_CO(1-0) using LVG model L'_CO(1-0) and three M_gas estimates (LVG, dust mass with GDMR=100, and [CI](2-1)); test alpha_CO vs T_dust correlation via MCMC linear fit and F-test; compute t_dep = M_gas / SFR; compare integrated CO cooling energy over t_dep with turbulent kinetic energy and stellar wind/supernova feedback energy.

evidence.quote: In SPT0311-58, we calculate $\rm \alpha_{CO}$ using three different estimates of gas mass as shown in Figure 12. The $\rm CO(1-0)$ luminosity is obtained from the *Turbulence* model where $\rm L^{\prime}_{CO(1-0)} = (8.3 \pm 1.3) \times 10^{10}\ K\ km\ s^{-1}\ pc^{2}$ in W and $\rm (8.8 \pm 2.6) \times 10^{9}\ K\ km\ s^{-1}\ pc^{2}$ in E.
The gas depletion time scale ($\rm t_{dep}$) is defined as $\rm M_{gas}/SFR$. We calculate and compare the depletion time scales in SPT0311-58 W and E with the literature sources in Figure 13.
The turbulent energy can be calculated from the turbulence line width and the gas mass (Table \[turb_parameters\]) as $\rm E_{turb} = 0.5\ M_{gas} \times dv_{turb}^{2}$.

key_parameters.value: F-test p-value < 0.05 for alpha_CO vs T_dust slope

evidence.quote: We use an F-test to determine that the model with a negative slope is statistically better than the model with no slope or zero correlation. We obtain a p$-$value of $<$ 0.05 and we reject the null hypothesis that the complex model i.e. the fit with negative slope does not provide more information than the fit with slope fixed to zero.

assumptions.value: GDMR = 100 for dust-based M_gas; Kroupa IMF with 0.2% O-type stars (10^49-51 erg over 5 Myr) and 7% supernova progenitors (10-40 M_sun, 10^51 erg each, <=1% efficiency to turbulence)

evidence.quote: We also calculate the gas mass from dust mass (Section 3.3) by assuming GDMR = 100 (cite: sandstrom13), which includes contribution from Helium.

Using an O-type stellar wind luminosity of $\sim 10^{49-51}$ ergs in a lifetime of 5 Myr (cite: leitherer99; smith14; ramachandran19) and assuming O-type stars comprise 0.2% of the total number of stars formed (Kroupa initial mass function), we can calculate the total energy output over the depletion time of the galaxies.

Stars with masses in the range of $\rm \sim 10-40\ M_{\odot}$ collapse as supernovae (cite: heger03), which emit an energy of $\sim 10^{51}$ ergs. Assuming the stars with these stellar masses comprise $\sim 7\%$ of the total stellar mass, we estimate a total energy output from supernovae explosions of $\sim 3 \times 10^{60}$ ergs in W and $\sim 2 \times 10^{59}$ ergs in E, over the depletion time scale.

fitting.value: MCMC linear fit of alpha_CO vs T_dust evaluated with an F-test

evidence.quote: We fit a linear function to the main sequence galaxies and the SPT-SMGs using MCMC and find a statistically significant correlation between $\rm \alpha_{CO}$ and $\rm T_{dust}$.

validation.value: Compared three independent methods for alpha_CO and two methods for t_dep

evidence.quote: In SPT0311-58, we calculate $\rm \alpha_{CO}$ using three different estimates of gas mass as shown in Figure 12.
We estimate $\rm t_{dep}$ in SPT0311-58 using two methods.

used_for.value: Data reduction pipeline, continuum subtraction (uvcontsub), and continuum and spectral line imaging

evidence.quote: The data reduction and imaging were performed using the Common Astronomy Software Application package `CASA` (cite: mcmullin07). We use the calibrated data products from the ALMA data reduction pipeline (`CASA` version 5.1.1).

To generate the spectral cubes, we use the same weighting as with the continuum maps and a velocity averaging of 100 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$, after subtracting the continuum using `CASA` task `uvcontsub` with a polynomial fit of order 1.

evidence.quote: Since the signal-to-noise is not sufficiently high for pixellated modeling, we use a parametric lens modeling code, `visilens` (cite: spilker16).

findings_qualitative.value: p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) is detected in SPT0311-58 W at z = 6.9, representing the most distant detection of water in a galaxy without any evidence for an AGN.

evidence.quote: This is the most detailed study of molecular gas content of a galaxy in the EoR to-date, with the most distant detection of $\rm H_{2}O$ in a galaxy without any evidence for active galactic nuclei in the literature.
We detect p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ in W with a signal-to-noise $\sim$4 above the continuum.

findings_qualitative.value: There is no significant differential magnification between the CO transitions and the dust continuum in SPT0311-58 W, and the CO emission region marginally decreases in size with increasing J level.

evidence.quote: From the top panel in Figure 11, we see that the magnification is consistent between the CO transitions and the dust continuum, i.e., we do not observe differential magnification between these components in SPT0311-58 W.
From the bottom panel of the figure, we see that the CO emission area is marginally decreasing with increasing excitation level.

findings_qualitative.value: The CO SLEDs of SPT0311-58 W and E peak at J_up ~ 6, typical of high-redshift starburst SMGs, while high L_CO(10-9)/L_CO(6-5) and T_kin/T_dust > 1 suggest mechanical heating in addition to photoelectric heating.

evidence.quote: Both the galaxies in SPT0311-58 peak at J$_{\rm up}$ $\sim$ 6, similar to other high-redshift starburst galaxies.

The ratio of $\rm T_{kin}/T_{dust}$ is $>$ 1 in both galaxies, which indicates that there are additional heating mechanisms such as X-rays, stellar outflows, and supernovae in addition to photoelectric heating in dense molecular gas.

findings_qualitative.value: There is a statistically significant negative correlation between alpha_CO and T_dust in main sequence galaxies and SPT-SMGs, and no evidence for evolution of gas depletion time with redshift in SMGs at z > 3.

evidence.quote: We fit a linear function to the main sequence galaxies and the SPT-SMGs using MCMC and find a statistically significant correlation between $\rm \alpha_{CO}$ and $\rm T_{dust}$.
We find no evidence of evolution of depletion time with redshift in SMGs at z $>$ 3.

claims.hypothesis: p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) emission at z = 6.9 follows the local and high-z L_H2O - L_FIR correlation and traces star formation rate.
claims.experiment: Measured p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) luminosity in SPT0311-58 W and E using ALMA Band 3, compared L_H2O/L_FIR against local and high-z ULIRGs via MCMC linear regression, and calibrated SFR from L_H2O.
claims.result: Detected p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) in W at SNR ~ 4 with I_obs = 0.97 +/- 0.09 Jy km s^-1; L_H2O/L_FIR = (1.10 +/- 0.4) x 10^-5; H2O-derived SFR in W is 4356 +/- 2143 M_sun/yr compared to L_IR-derived SFR of 5046 +/- 944 M_sun/yr.
claims.finding: The L_H2O/L_FIR ratio in SPT0311-58 is consistent with other high-redshift ULIRGs, and H2O-derived SFR agrees with L_IR-derived SFR within uncertainties.

evidence.quote: The p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ luminosity in SPT0311-58 W and E is consistent within the scatter of the other high-redshift ULIRGs.

From the $\rm L_{H_{2}O}$-$\rm L_{FIR}$ correlation, we estimate a SFR of $\rm 4356 \pm 2143\ M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ in W and an upper limit of $\rm 385\ M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ in E. The SFR calculated from $\rm L_{IR}$ is $\rm 5046 \pm 944\ M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ in W and $\rm 701 \pm 151\ M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ in E.

claims.hypothesis: Differential magnification across CO transitions and dust continuum could bias the derived CO SLED and physical properties in SPT0311-58 W.
claims.experiment: Performed parametric visibility-plane lens modeling with visilens on 95 GHz and 140 GHz continuum and CO(6-5), CO(7-6), and CO(10-9) emission in W.
claims.result: Derived magnifications of 2.09 +/- 0.06 (95 GHz), 2.09 +/- 0.10 (140 GHz), 2.08 +/- 0.21 (CO 6-5), 2.13 +/- 0.14 (CO 7-6), and 2.16 +/- 0.11 (CO 10-9), with CO emission size marginally decreasing with J_up.
claims.finding: There is no significant differential magnification between the CO transitions and the dust continuum in SPT0311-58 W.

evidence.quote: From the top panel in Figure 11, we see that the magnification is consistent between the CO transitions and the dust continuum, i.e., we do not observe differential magnification between these components in SPT0311-58 W.

claims.hypothesis: Heating mechanisms in addition to photoelectric heating (such as mechanical heating from turbulence, stellar winds, and supernovae) contribute to the high-J CO excitation in SPT0311-58.
claims.experiment: Compared L_[CII]/L_FIR vs L_CO(10-9)/L_CO(6-5) against local and high-z samples, modeled T_kin/T_dust with non-LTE Turbulence LVG radiative transfer, and compared integrated CO cooling energy over t_dep with turbulent kinetic energy and stellar/SN feedback energy.
claims.result: Found high L_CO(10-9)/L_CO(6-5) comparable to Class II/III galaxies, T_kin/T_dust = 2.0 +/- 0.9 (W) and 3.4 +/- 1.3 (E), and turbulent energy (~10^59 erg in W, ~10^57 erg in E) matching total CO cooling energy (~5x10^58 erg in W, ~3x10^57 erg in E).
claims.finding: Additional heating mechanisms beyond photoelectric heating are present, and mechanical heating from star formation (stellar outflows and supernovae cascading into turbulence) can account for the CO cooling budget without requiring an AGN.

evidence.quote: $\rm T_{kin}/T_{dust} = 2.0 \pm 0.9$ and $3.4 \pm 1.3$ in SPT0311-58 W and E, respectively, which suggests that there are other heating mechanisms in addition to photoelectric heating (traced by $\rm T_{dust}$).
We get a turbulence energy of $\rm \sim 1 \times 10^{59}\ ergs$ in W and $\rm \sim 1 \times 10^{57}\ ergs$ in E, similar to the total CO cooling energy.

The mechanical heating from stellar outflows and supernovae explosions, some of which is converted into turbulent energy, may contribute significantly to the total CO cooling over the depletion timescale.

claims.hypothesis: The CO-to-H2 conversion factor (alpha_CO) and gas depletion timescale (t_dep) in SPT0311-58 at z = 6.9 are consistent with lower-redshift SMGs, and t_dep does not evolve with redshift in SMGs at z > 3.
claims.experiment: Derived M_gas, alpha_CO, and t_dep in SPT0311-58 W and E from Turbulence LVG modeling, dust mass, and [CI](2-1), and compared them with a re-analyzed literature sample of SMGs and SPT-SMGs across redshift.
claims.result: Obtained alpha_CO = 7.1 +/- 5.3 (W) and 3.9 +/- 4.4 (E) from the Turbulence model (1.6 +/- 0.7 and 2.1 +/- 0.9 from dust mass; sample mean 3.2 +/- 2.7), and t_dep = 107 +/- 70 Myr (W) and 44 +/- 40 Myr (E) with flat t_dep distribution at z > 3.
claims.finding: alpha_CO and t_dep in SPT0311-58 are consistent with high-redshift SMGs within uncertainties, and there is no evidence of t_dep evolution with redshift in SMGs at z > 3.

evidence.quote: The CO-to-H2 conversion factor ($\rm \alpha_{CO}$) and the gas depletion time scales estimated from the model are consistent with the high-redshift SMGs in the literature within the uncertainties. We find no evidence of evolution of depletion time with redshift in SMGs at z $>$ 3.

However, this evolution does not seem to exist in the SMG sample at z $>$ 3. In SPT0311-58 W and E, the depletion time obtained from both the methods are within the typical range for high-redshift SMGs.

why_this_data.value: High-resolution ALMA Band 3 and 4 observations spatially resolve SPT0311-58 into West and East and sample mid-J CO, high-J CO(10-9), [CI](2-1), and p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) to constrain the ISM density, temperature, gas mass, and heating mechanisms at z = 6.9.

evidence.quote: In this paper, we combine the previous observations with high resolution molecular line imaging with ALMA, including the high-J CO transition, $\rm CO(10-9)$ and p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$.
For the continuum flux density in B3, we use the current observations which are at a higher resolution of $\sim$0.5$''$ compared to previous observations at $\sim$3.5$''$.

why_this_method.value: Used [CII] template fitting because lines are non-Gaussian and blended; used parametric visibility-plane lens modeling (visilens) because SNR is insufficient for pixellated reconstruction and to account for correlated noise; used Turbulence non-LTE LVG modeling to realistically represent a continuous log-normal density distribution in turbulent gas with fewer parameters than a 2-component model.

evidence.quote: Since the spectral lines are non-Gaussian and blended in the case of $\rm CO(7-6)$ and \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$, and $\rm CO(10-9)$ and p-$\rm H_{2} O (3_{1,2}-2_{2,1})$, we use \[CII\] from the ALMA 240 GHz observations (cite: marrone18) as a template to derive the spectral properties.
Since the signal-to-noise is not sufficiently high for pixellated modeling, we use a parametric lens modeling code, `visilens` (cite: spilker16).
The analysis is performed in the visibility plane instead of the image plane to account for the correlated noise in the interferometric images.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Pixellated lensing reconstruction was not used for the new continuum and CO datasets because the signal-to-noise ratio is not sufficiently high.

evidence.quote: Since the signal-to-noise is not sufficiently high for pixellated modeling, we use a parametric lens modeling code, `visilens` (cite: spilker16).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: 1-component and 2-component LVG models were run alongside the Turbulence model, and N > 2 components were avoided due to increased degeneracies from additional free parameters.

evidence.quote: However, due to the increased degeneracies with increased number of free parameters, we use 1 and 2 components in this analysis.

limitations_admitted.value: CO(3-2) from ATCA is spatially unresolved (5-6'') between W and E and had to be distributed by scaling to CO(6-5).

evidence.quote: Since $\rm CO(3-2)$ is spatially unresolved ($\sim$5 $-$ 6$''$) into W and E, we distribute the flux density of $\rm CO(3-2)$ by scaling to $\rm CO(6-5)$ in the two galaxies.

limitations_admitted.value: Signal-to-noise is insufficient for lensing reconstruction in E and for p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) in W, requiring adoption of fixed magnification factors from Marrone et al. (2018).

evidence.quote: Since we do not have a good signal-to-noise for lensing reconstruction in E, we adopt a magnification of 1.3 for all the molecular lines. For the same reason, we adopt $\mu = 2.2$ from (cite: marrone18) in p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ in W.

limitations_admitted.value: [CI](2-1) and p-H2O(2_1,1-2_0,2) are not significantly detected in E, and the lack of [CI](1-0) observations prevents direct measurement of the [CI] excitation temperature and confirmation of the [CI] abundance-density relation.

evidence.quote: However, it has to be noted that, due to the lack of \[CI\]$\rm (1-0)$ observations, we cannot reliably confirm the relationship between \[CI\] abundance and gas density.
The non-detection of \[CI\]$\rm (2-1)$ and p-$\rm H_{2} O (2_{1,1}-2_{0,2})$ in E gives large uncertainty on the depletion time estimate.

limitations_admitted.value: In the LVG models, T_kin/T_dust is assumed constant across all visual extinctions/densities rather than varying with extinction or density.

evidence.quote: However, it has to be noted that, while T$_{\rm K}$/T$_{\rm dust}$ is a function of visual extinction (cite: tielens85), we consider a constant value at all extinctions.
One caveat is that we do not consider the change in $\rm T_{kin}$/$\rm T_{dust}$ with density in the LVG model.

limitations_admitted.value: Observations of important neutral gas coolants [OI] (63 um) and [SiII] (35 um), which contribute >50% of total cooling, are unavailable.

evidence.quote: However, since we do not have observations of the two important coolants \[OI\] and \[SiII\], which are found to contribute to more than 50% of the total cooling budget (cite: rosenberg15), we cannot provide the complete picture of the neutral gas.

referee_caveats_inferred: Distributing unresolved ATCA CO(3-2) flux between W and E using the CO(6-5) ratio assumes identical CO(6-5)/CO(3-2) excitation in both galaxies, which directly affects the low-J CO SLED and LVG-derived L'_CO(1-0).

Deblending CO(7-6)+[CI](2-1) and CO(10-9)+p-H2O(3_1,2-2_2,1) by fixing the line profiles to the [CII] 158 um template assumes that high-J CO, [CI], and H2O share the exact same spatial/kinematic distribution as [CII].

Two different dust mass absorption coefficient normalizations are used in the paper: kappa_nu = 0.038 * (nu/372.7 GHz)^beta in Section 3.3 vs kappa_nu = 0.04 * (nu/250 GHz)^beta in Section 4.4, which introduces a systematic offset between MBB and LVG dust masses.

The empirical correlation between alpha_CO and T_dust is derived using M_dust and T_dust fitted from the same FIR photometry assuming a fixed GDMR = 100, creating correlated errors between the two axes.

data_public_as_stated.value: ALMA project codes 2017.1.01168, 2016.1.01293, and 2015.1.00504.S and Herschel ID DDT_mstrande_1 are stated

evidence.quote: This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA #2017.1.01168, ADS/JAO.ALMA #2016.1.01293, and ADS/JAO.ALMA #2015.1.00504.S.
We also include *Herschel*/SPIRE photometry at 250, 350, and 500 $\mu$m (project ID: DDT$\_$mstrande$\_$1, (cite: strandet16)).

products_in_archive.value: Calibrated data products from the ALMA data reduction pipeline (CASA v5.1.1) were used

evidence.quote: We use the calibrated data products from the ALMA data reduction pipeline (`CASA` version 5.1.1).

missing_for_reproduction: The non-LTE LVG radiative transfer codes (N-component and Turbulence) and the Monte Carlo Bees Algorithm implementation are not publicly linked or released in the paper.
Appendix Tables (FIR photometry table and best-fit values in Tables 4, 5, and 6 for lens modeling) are missing or truncated in the provided manuscript text.
Exact CASA imaging parameters (cell size, image size, stopping threshold, clean masks) and exact spectral extraction aperture centers are not stated.
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~20-50 GB (calibrated measurement sets for 3 tunings in ALMA project 2017.1.01168.S plus ancillary [CII] Band 6 dataset from 2016.1.01293.S)
reproducibility.score_reason: The observational setup, calibration provenance (standard ALMA pipeline in CASA 5.1.1), spectral template fitting, modified blackbody SED equations, and LVG model equations/priors are thoroughly documented, and visilens/emcee are public. However, the custom Turbulence/N-component LVG radiative transfer code is not publicly released, and several imaging/aperture details and Appendix table entries are incomplete in the text.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: All ALMA project codes are public in the archive, standard pipeline calibration was used, visilens is open-source, and key numeric results (continuum fluxes, line fluxes via [CII] template deblending, lensing magnifications, MBB dust masses/temperatures, and [CI]/H2O-based gas mass and SFR) can be independently reproduced from the archival data.

methods_papers.why: Parametric visibility-plane gravitational lens modeling code visilens and lambda_0 - T_dust relation
Modified blackbody dust SED equations and foundational non-LTE LVG radiative transfer equations
Updated N-component non-LTE LVG radiative transfer model
Turbulence non-LTE LVG radiative transfer model and turbulent/stellar feedback energy budget framework
Monte Carlo Bees Algorithm used to optimize the LVG radiative transfer models

companion_papers.why: Discovery of z = 6.9 redshift and unresolved low/mid-J CO analysis of SPT0311-58
High-resolution ALMA dust, [CII], and [OIII] observations and pixellated lens modeling of SPT0311-58
